title: India Orders States to Set Up Special Drug Courts as 3.96 Lakh Cases Pile Up
excerpt: The Ministry of Home Affairs has directed all states to establish exclusive courts under the NDPS Act, as high courts across India lose patience with a backlog that has paralyzed narcotics prosecutions.
body:
• The Centre has directed all states to establish exclusive courts under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act to clear 3.96 lakh pending drug cases nationwide.
  • High courts in Kerala, Jammu & Kashmir, Gujarat, and West Bengal have issued separate orders criticizing state governments for failing to comply with a 2013 Supreme Court directive on special NDPS courts.
  • Union Home Minister Amit Shah called the anti-drug campaign a "sacred mission" and pushed for fast-track prosecution, stronger forensic labs, and aggressive asset confiscation of drug traffickers.
  • Kerala alone has over 7,200 pending NDPS cases, and its High Court has ordered five new special courts to be operationalized within three months with permanent staff.

India's Ministry of Home Affairs has directed all states and union territories to urgently set up exclusive courts for trying cases under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, citing a staggering backlog of 3.96 lakh pending drug cases across the country, according to The Indian Express. The directive follows mounting pressure from high courts, which have accused state governments of dragging their feet on a Supreme Court order issued more than a decade ago.

A Decade of Inaction

The Supreme Court's 2013 judgment in Thana Singh v. Central Bureau of Narcotics ordered every state, in consultation with its High Court, to establish special courts that would deal exclusively with NDPS offences. The number of courts was to be proportionate to the volume of pending cases. Until these courts were set up, NDPS cases were to be prioritized over all other matters.

Thirteen years later, compliance remains patchy. In West Bengal, the Calcutta High Court noted that "no effort has been made by the State government" to establish such courts, according to LiveLaw. In Gujarat, only one of four notified special NDPS courts was functioning, the High Court observed. In Jammu & Kashmir, the High Court said the Supreme Court's directions had "fallen on deaf ears" and accused successive governments of having "dragged their feet."

Kerala Leads the Judicial Push

Kerala's High Court has emerged as the most aggressive in forcing action. With 7,202 NDPS cases pending across the state as of March 2025 — and pendency growing threefold from the previous year — Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice C. Jayachandran directed the state to operationalize five new special NDPS courts within three months. The courts are to be established in Thiruvananthapuram, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Palakkad, and Manjeri.

The Kerala bench also insisted on permanent staffing, rejecting the state's plan to fill positions on a contractual basis. "These courts deal with confidential intelligence and matters relating to witness protection, which demand institutional loyalty and long-term accountability," the court observed, according to LiveLaw.

The court further directed Kerala to seek central financial assistance under the Scheme for Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment, with the Deputy Solicitor General confirming the state could still apply even though formal timelines had expired.

Shah's "Sacred Mission"

At a Regional Conference on Drug Trafficking and National Security, Union Home Minister Amit Shah framed the campaign against narcotics as existential. "Our campaign against drug abuse is a sacred mission to save the future generations of the country," he said, according to ANI.

Shah pushed for harsher punishment, faster prosecution, and aggressive asset confiscation. He also demanded that states strengthen their Forensic Science Laboratories. "Until we strengthen the FSLs, the prosecution will not progress," he said, calling it "a question of initiative, not resources."

"Until we strengthen the Forensic Science Labs, the prosecution will not progress. This is a question of initiative, not resources."

— Amit Shah, Union Home Minister

At the same event, the Narcotics Control Bureau destroyed over 1.40 lakh kilograms of seized narcotics worth Rs 2,378 crore in a single day — a record. Drug seizures between 2014 and 2023 rose 160 percent to 3.94 lakh kilograms compared to the preceding eight-year period, Shah said, with registered cases jumping 200 percent.

Systemic Bottlenecks

The backlog is not merely a question of court capacity. Forensic science labs are severely understaffed. In Kerala, the State Police Chief proposed 31 new posts for FSLs, but only 12 were sanctioned. The Kerala High Court has separately urged the Centre to consider establishing a Central Forensic Science Laboratory (CFSL) in the state — there are currently only six in the entire country.

The Supreme Court has also waded into the broader issue. In a related suo motu matter on delays in special criminal trials, the bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi ordered exclusive NIA courts for cases under the UAPA and NDPS Act. Additional Solicitor General SD Sanjay told the court that the proposal for exclusive NDPS courts was "under active consideration" and that "substantial administrative progress" had been made, according to India Legal.

What's Next

Haryana has moved faster than most, adding 13 fast-track NDPS courts across the state. But for the majority of states, implementation remains on paper. The Kerala High Court's next hearing is scheduled for June 24, and it has made clear that further delays will not be tolerated.

With nearly four lakh cases languishing in overloaded sessions courts — and conviction rates in drug cases historically low due to procedural delays — the MHA directive adds central weight to what has so far been a piecemeal judicial effort. Whether states respond with the urgency the situation demands remains the open question.
nri_angle: Nearly four lakh pending drug cases clog India's courts, undermining faith in the justice system for NRIs with property disputes or family cases that share overburdened court dockets.
